title: The Pod Save America episode titled "The 3.5% Protest Rule That Could Bring Trump Down," aired…
text:
The Pod Save America episode titled "The 3.5% Protest Rule That Could Bring Trump Down," aired on June 10, 2025, features political scientist Erica Chenoweth discussing her research on nonviolent protest movements and the "3.5% rule." Hosted by former Obama aides Jon Favreau, Jon Lovett, Dan Pfeiffer, and Tommy Vietor, this episode explores how mass nonviolent resistance could challenge authoritarian tendencies, specifically in the context of Donald Trump’s political influence. 

The episode centers on Erica Chenoweth’s concept of the "3.5% rule," which posits that no government in the past century has withstood a nonviolent protest movement that actively engages at least 3.5% of a country’s population. Chenoweth, a renowned scholar of nonviolent resistance, joins the hosts to discuss how this principle could apply to countering perceived authoritarian actions by Donald Trump, particularly in the context of his political resurgence or policies post-2024 election. The conversation is framed as a hopeful and actionable discussion, emphasizing strategies for grassroots mobilization to protect democratic norms.

title: How many ways can we say this is not the correct approach or style to address the obvious…
text: How many ways can we say this is not the correct approach or style to address the obvious problems of debt, trade deficit, "hollowed out" US manufacturing base, etc. Those are real problems that require thoughtful solutions using both history and sound econ 101 principles. The globe is deeply interconnected. US has 5% of the world's population yet controls 30% of the overall global GDP. The wealth disparity across the globe and wage expectations are such that market forces will gravitate towards efficiency. Other parts of the world will use every tool possible to push back. Recreating a mythic pre-WW 2 economy is foolish.So, what to do? We need a forward-looking strategy and 1. shore up our allies, 2. Be strategic and decide what types of advanced manufacturing we can truly and efficiently corner the world on (not making underwear) such as CHIPS, 3. Aggressively invest in our people and skills needed for this future, and, 4. get our politics in order so we are hating each other (50% split of what day of week it is). This is hard work, and I am not sure we have leadership or discipline to get this done. The current approach is not the way to success (imho).  We need an attitude of "make America great yet allow others to thrive as well."  The zero-sum mindset is not going to be accepted, unless you are prepared to use unilateral force.https://www.wsj.com/opinion/auto-industry-tariffs-china-cars-ford-stellantis-tesla-donald-trump-ef7e235a?st=GYmets&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink

title: I wish to voice some thoughts as I have been paying attention to the Collingswood's local…
text: I wish to voice some thoughts as I have been paying attention to the Collingswood's local issues, including the school district's financial challenges, potential for property tax increases, and the upcoming commissioner's race. My reflections are those of a relative newcomer with no kids in the school system, attracted to the area for the local "vibe" and charm.I reviewed the school system’s latest performance report. The demographics indicate the majority is non-white (53%), economically disadvantaged represents 38%, and special needs 16%. The performance metrics are what they are. As I have attended several town hall meetings and BOE meetings, the audience does NOT reflect the demographics of the school. Also, the agenda and priorities seem distant from reality on the ground.There is no “judgment” here, but a genuine concern as to the state of affairs and how sustainable this is.  Clearly, participation by those with a stake is critical and I wonder what efforts are being made to address this. At last night’s “Candidate’s Election Forum” there were many statements made about “diversity” but there was no serious discussion about these sensitive issues.  If there are forums where this happens, please refer me to those!  My goal in stating out loud what may be obvious to others is to encourage discussion, as I do not know a lot about the borough.  Is there a material difference in approach to these issues by the different candidates? https://www.collsk12.org/article/2126726

title: I see a lot of frustration and snark amongst my liberal colleagues, posting the latest outrage…
text:
I see a lot of frustration and snark amongst my liberal colleagues, posting the latest outrage from Trump, Musk et al.  I am sympathetic but I find most of it off-putting and not very effective (perhaps humorous and feel like we’re doing something).  I found the recent episode helpful of Ezra Klein discussing with David Shor, the head of data science at Blue Rose Research, a Democratic polling firm, which does an enormous amount of surveying of the electorate. 
This is highly data driven and was enlightening as to why Tump won and the messages for the democratic party. They are desperately being outflanked on social media (tik tok), amongst the young, men, latinos, working class (without a college degree), and tech elites.  This will be a problem they may not be able to solve easily.  So what are potential solutions??

title: Well it’s been 50 days and my head is spinning trying to follow the fire hose of recent news…
text:
Well it’s been 50 days and my head is spinning trying to follow the fire hose of recent news coming out and alarm from friends from around the world. Trying to separate overreaction from liberals from genuine concern has been difficult.  Many of the issues and orders will be litigated and even trying to follow along will require study of con law and arcane jurisprudence: 
Stare decisis (Precedent), 
Humphrey’s Executor, 
Decision of 1789,
Impoundment Authority. and
Unitary executive theory.  

To assist in this journey is an excellent podcast that addresses the current issues in a thoughtful, humorous, and with sarcasm (Strict Scrutiny).  This is an ongoing weekly series. Not for the faint of heart!

title: Tax policy is exceptionally boring and difficult to understand.
text:
Tax policy is exceptionally boring and difficult to understand. However, in a world where national debt and deficits and shutting down government agencies are top of mind, we have to pay attention to this source of revenue to the system.
In December 2024, Jessica Riedl, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute (a center right org, previously was at the heritage institute, and was an economist for Rob Portman of Ohio), published a report titled “Correcting the Top 10 Tax Myths,” aiming to dispel common misconceptions about the U.S. federal tax system.
Jessica is critical of both sides of the aisle in their policies for the past 25 years. The Freakonomics podcast explores a variety of issues in a thoughtful manner.
The ten myths addressed are:
1. “Tax Cuts Pay for Themselves”
The belief that tax cuts entirely offset their revenue losses through stimulated economic growth is challenged; while tax cuts can boost the economy, they seldom fully compensate for the initial revenue reduction.
2. “Tax Cuts Will Starve the Beast”
The notion that reducing tax revenue will force the government to cut spending is disputed; historical evidence indicates that spending often continues to rise despite tax cuts.
3. “The Middle Class Pays Higher Tax Rates than the Rich”
Contrary to this claim, the U.S. federal tax system is progressive, with higher-income individuals generally paying higher effective tax rates than middle-class taxpayers.
4. “Those Old 91% Tax Rates Raised Large Tax Revenues”
The high marginal tax rates of the 1950s are often cited as effective revenue generators; however, due to numerous deductions and loopholes, the effective tax rates were much lower, resulting in less revenue than presumed.
5. “Europe’s Higher Tax Revenues Derive from Aggressively Taxing the Rich”
European countries achieve higher tax revenues primarily through broad-based taxes like value-added taxes (VAT), which affect all citizens, not solely through high taxes on the wealthy.
6. ”âTax Cuts for the Rich’ Drive Soaring Budget Deficits”
While tax cuts can contribute to deficits, attributing large budget deficits solely to tax reductions for the wealthy overlooks the significant impact of increased government spending.
7. “Taxing Millionaires and Corporations Can Eliminate the Deficit”
Relying exclusively on taxing high-income individuals and corporations is insufficient to close the deficit; comprehensive fiscal solutions require broader tax strategies and spending reforms.
8. “Most of the 2017 Tax Cuts Went to Corporations and the Wealthy”
Analysis shows that the 2017 tax cuts provided benefits across various income groups, not exclusively favoring corporations and high-income individuals.
9. “Repealing All Post-1980 Tax Cuts Provides Painless Deficit Reduction”
Simply reversing tax cuts enacted since 1980 is not a straightforward solution for deficit reduction, as it would involve significant tax increases affecting a wide range of taxpayers.
10. “America’s Corporate Taxes Are Far Below International Standards”
The perception that U.S. corporate taxes are much lower than international norms is misleading; when considering state and local taxes, U.S. corporate tax rates are comparable to those in other developed countries.
Riedl’s report emphasizes the importance of grounding tax policy debates in accurate data and comprehensive analysis to avoid perpetuating these myths.

title: Democrats are deeply frustrated and in the wilderness as they see many policies they have…
text:
Democrats are deeply frustrated and in the wilderness as they see many policies they have championed or care about being dismantled.  However, one notable exception maybe the work of Lena Kahn at the FTC in her pursuit of holding big corporations accountable.  Though she was vilified by many in corporate circles (i.e. WSJ) and she was replaced in the administration, her legacy seems to live on with surprising bipartisan interest.  

Shoutout to a recent episode of the Freakonomics podcast.

title: This is the tension in America today, the balance between oversight & regulation vs.
text:
This is the tension in America today, the balance between oversight & regulation vs. free market and for profit.  This is playing out in all sectors, and nowhere more personal than in our healthcare. The recent national election winds are blowing in the direction of less regulation. However, this heinous murder of Thompson (CEO of UHC) in NYC maybe a watershed moment that crystalizes a backlash against our current system of health insurance coverage. Beyond the obvious immorality of murder, the outrage against the industry is unlike anything I have seen before (the multitude of responses to this op-ed by the CEO of UHG are impassioned).  Holding the industry accountable will require a strong response from the gov't (anti-trust regulators, etc.) as it likely has not and will not happen by itself?

I will share a personal anecdote. My 28 y/o son is a "gig worker", is not covered on our employer-sponsored health plan and he does not have health insurance. I shopped for health insurance during this open enrollment period on the exchange. I signed him up (healthy young man) for the cheapest plan available (IBX Independence Keystone HMO for $230/month premium). The annual deductible is a whopping $8,000, out-of-pocket cap is $9,000/yr.  In what world does this make economic sense? This is basically catastrophic coverage.  Aso, it is a negative incentive to seek healthcare! 

All healthcare solutions have to be geared to the societal ethos and in that sense I don’t think that a single payer universal system (as in Canada or Europe) is feasible in the US.  With 20% of GDP and entrenched private corporate interests and deep suspicion by the public of anything the gov’t does indicates need for other US-centric approaches (i.e. market competition). We as a society will need to figure this out, hopefully at the ballot box rather than in the streets!

title: I would consider myself as an "institutionalist" and have largely been aghast at efforts to…
text:
I would consider myself as an "institutionalist" and have largely been aghast at efforts to discredit our institutions writ large. However, we all need to have an open mind and not simply adhere to a tribe! 

I was onboard with the mainstream scientific consensus and was (and am) a supporter of the NIH / CDC and Fauci, largely based on a sense of an existential threat to the public of a newly discovered covid-19 virus, etc. and I supported lockdowns. Looking at the policies now in retrospect, a wholesale shutdown of society was an overreaction and is not consistent with typical approach to care, which is usually based on relative background risk (i.e. young and healthy are at vanishingly low risk c/w the elderly and compromised).  How a risk-based strategy may have fared is an open question and experts will grapple with that further. But clearly, more than science played a significant role in public policy!

This is a story of a physician scientist (Dr. Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford) who went against the grain in 2021 (published the Great Barrington Declaration in 2020 which advocated lifting lockdowns and "herd immunity"), was vilified, and now is the nominee for the NIH, the most prestigious biomedical research grantor. Jay appears to be an unconventional yet critical thinker, but not a quack (important distinction). He also has interesting and important views on the staid "old guard" in science, group think or mob mentality, and academic fraud, and the centrality of reproducibility of findings in science. This is a key space to monitor as to how Dr. Bhattacharya navigates the scientific "swamp" and the research and journal publishing culture that is currently extant.

I am not yet ready to take a similarly open-minded approach to other institutions under assault.

title: Just finished Yuval Noah Harari's 2024 book, "Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks…
text:
Just finished Yuval Noah Harari's 2024 book, "Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI". The book examines how humans have historically used information networks to cooperate, gain power, and shape societies. It also explores the challenges posed by the rise of artificial intelligence and the spread of misinformation.
The book was dense, full of references to history and how information networks evolved and were utilized. Harari, dating back to his earlier book Homo Sapiens, is a strong believer in the concept of stories, narratives, and myths as organizing principles in human history (that separate us from the other great apes). 

Key Themes:

1. Evolution of Information Networks: Harari traces the development of communication systems from early human societies (i.e. oral history, hand written church texts, printing press and printed bibles) to today's AI-driven networks, emphasizing how shared beliefs (even myths) have united large groups and enabled cooperation.

2. Dual Nature of Information: Information can serve both constructive and destructive purposes. The book highlights the complexity of distinguishing truth from fiction, especially in an era of AI-augmented narratives.

3. AI’s Role and Risks: Harari warns that AI, with intelligence untethered from human consciousness, poses existential risks. While AI can enhance efficiency and connectivity, it also raises concerns about manipulation, inequality, and the potential loss of human autonomy.

4. Human Agency in the AI Era: Harari stresses the urgency of making ethical and informed decisions about AI governance, arguing that these choices will determine humanity's future in the face of transformative technological change.

5. Historical Parallels: Through examples like witch hunts, totalitarian regimes, and modern populism, Harari illustrates how information networks have shaped societal dynamics and highlights the dangers of centralized information control.

"Nexus" serves as both a historical analysis and a cautionary tale, urging society to navigate the intersection of technology, information, and power thoughtfully. It highlights the potential for AI to either deepen cooperation or exacerbate societal divides depending on its use.

The book was highly informative about history, less so about current AI technology or specific winners or losers. He emphasizes "self-correcting networks" as a key factor separating benevolent forces from those that are not and prone to destruction (i.e. Hitler's world view). There are references to our current political state as well as a future of bot-on-bot world!  The second half of book was more relevant to current affairs. Also, there was a preachy tone and finger wagging in certain sections!

title: I just read this excellent book (Age of Revolutions, Fareed Zakaria), which coincided with our…
text:
I just read this excellent book (Age of Revolutions, Fareed Zakaria), which coincided with our national elections. Sometimes we get lost in the current day politics, but it helps to consider a longer-term perspective. In Part 1, Zakaria contextualizes 5 major past revolutions shaping the western world: Liberal revolution of the Netherlands, the Glorious (blood-less) revolution extending to England, the failed French revolution, the Industrial revolution in Britain as well as the parallel one in the US. He compares and contrasts these revolutions from the standpoint of liberalism vs. control by a king or the church. In Part 2, Zakaria posits there are 4 major current revolutions shaping the modern world: globalization (economics), information overload (technology), identitarian (tribal), and geopolitics. 

I found the discussion extremely educational as he frequently quotes from well-known thinkers; the section on American history itself was incisive. He takes vague references to more concretely discuss in detail (i.e. China Shock, Bretton Woods and the Washington Concensus, New Deal vs. neoliberal order, gunboat diplomacy, role of Luddites, Tocqueville, 5 stages of Vernon, etc.).  Of course, there was a lot of name-dropping for further study!  The timing of this book presages the contentious 2024 US election, and the unique role Trump is playing in scrambling current day politics.  

Zakaria is a current scholar & historian who takes a pragmatic approach to the world order.  I find him to be a sober thinker, especially as it pertains to the role of America in the current world order.

title: As some of you know, I follow Ezra Klein's podcasts and columns closely, beyond the petty…
text: As some of you know, I follow Ezra Klein's podcasts and columns closely, beyond the petty politics of which team is going to win the election, etc. From a historical standpoint trying to understand the realignment that is taking place.  Recent episode featured a probing discussion of the American world order, from the New Deal of FDR (prevalent from 30s thru 60s with emphasis on social safety net), the rise of "neo-liberal" order from Regan till 2008 (with emphasis on freedom and free markets till the financial crisis), and the current inchoate phase. We can no longer think in terms of left vs. right, liberal vs conservative, corporate vs. worker, etc.  A bigger model is faith in institutions vs. a different order yet to be defined.  The issue of what (who) to trust is really preeminent (certainly not the traditional media, social media, courts, neighbors, bosses, military leaders, FBI, intelligence agencies, DOJ, CDC, HHS, etc.). Perhaps billionaires? This is much more disorienting than supporting "your team." Historical perspective helps us to think beyond election cycles and longer term! ð
